newsitem.title: UK: Coffee reignites as producers extend quotas.
newsitem.headline: Coffee reignites as producers extend quotas.

text.p: A spectacular rally in world coffee prices was reignited on Wednesday when producing nations agreed to extend their current cartel-style export quotas for 12 At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, arabica coffee futures for July rose to $2.55 per pound then closed at $2.53 which was up by a hefty 13 cents on the day.

The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC), anxious to defend prices after the present fever in the market abates, ended London talks with an accord to limit total exports by the 14 members to 52.75 million (60 kg) bags for the 12 months from July 1.
This is about the same as the volume limit that they had set under current curbs expiring June 30. A statement said the goal was "to ensure prices remain at a level remunerative to producers".
The deal was cut against a backdrop of a rally that has taken benchmark futures prices for green (unroasted) beans up 80-100 percent since January.
The price is strong because of low stocks and tight Latin American supply in the run-up to the time of year when Brazil, the biggest exporter, is at risk of winter frosts.
But Wednesday's firmer New York price at around $2.55 for July delivery arabica beans was somewhat below a 20-year high at $2.80 to which the now-expired May contract had risen a few days ago.

And the ACPC is worried that speculative funds could suddenly cash in their gains on the rally and send the market down again, particularly at the end of the Brazilian winter in about 15 weeks' time - if there is no frost to damage the crop there.

Officials of consumer governments privately said they were surprised at the ACPC decision to keep quotas now. But Brazilian traders reacted with approval, predicting that, if there is no frost damage, Brazil may have a bumper crop next year in excess of 30 million bags.
The ACPC made clear, however, that it does not want high prices to quench consumer demand for coffee, so it made provision to juggle supply within the one-year limit in line with fluctuating demand.

A technical group will monitor conditions and a seasonal allocation of quotas will not be made until September. The aim was a price that ensured a fair return to exporters' economies "but allowing continuing growth in worldwide consumption of coffee".

Although prices kicked higher on the ACPC news, several traders said the decisions were somewhat academic just now, with the market scrambling for every bean it can get and exporters disposed to ignore quotas and sell whatever they can.
"I don't think this should have an effect on the market," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "I don't think it's an overly effective programme anyway."
But brokerage GNI Ltd said in a commentary that the real test of the ACPC would be how it behaves "when prices fall if the Brazilian crop survives frost damage this winter"

"The ACPC news is being taken in a supportive fashion," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt in the United States. "It still shows a united front by the ACPC by standing together and not changing quotas."

Traders on the New York floor also attributed the market's new upswing to weather outlooks calling for cooler temperatures in Brazil this weekend. Forecasters say the colder air is not expected to cause damage but any drop in temperatures causes jitters.
